one_liner: Nim's checked release build with the clang backend runs fannkuch-redux(8) 1.13x faster than the best C build; with the gcc backend it loses.
what_it_does: This is a row from LangArena, a 50-task, 26-language benchmark suite, not a library. CLBG::Fannkuchredux enumerates all 8! = 40,320 permutations of 8 elements in counting-rotation order, counts the pancake flips for each, and returns a checksum and the maximum flip count. It runs 700 timed calls after 140 warm-up calls, with n read from run.js at runtime. The Nim version (nim/src/benchmarks/fannkuchredux.nim) follows the C version loop for loop over fixed 32-element stack arrays. The suite checksum 135762480 (840 calls x 161,622, derived) is checked for every language.
how_it_is_fast: No language mechanism is behind this: it is a codegen difference between two equivalent C programs built by the same LLVM 22.1.8 (the nim_clang and clang_c Docker images both start FROM langarena:base_clang). In the source, the hand-written C copies the permutation with memcpy(perm, perm1, n*sizeof(int)) at a runtime length for each of the 40,320 permutations, swaps through a pointer helper, and uses 32-bit int. Nim emits a plain element-copy loop over 64-bit ints, with -d:release keeping bound and overflow checks. Per permutation that is 32.5 ns for Nim/Clang against 36.7 ns for C/Gcc and 41.6 ns for C/Clang (derived from page data over 28.2M timed permutations). Untested hypothesis (assembly not inspected): the runtime checks stop clang from turning the copy loop into a memcpy call or from vectorising and unrolling loops of at most 8 iterations, which helps here.
when_to_use: Nim kernels over small fixed-size integer arrays with short inner loops (permutation enumeration, combinatorial search) built with the stock -d:release flags and --cc:clang: the checked build matched or beat hand-written C here.

Evidence that Nim's default runtime checks need not cost speed on such loops: the checked Nim/Clang build (0.918-0.933 s) beat the unchecked -d:danger build (1.114-1.146 s) in all five monthly runs checked (2026-07-14 to 2026-10-05).
Picking a Nim backend for integer loop kernels: clang (0.918 s) and NLVM (0.944 s) beat gcc (1.116 s) on the same Nim source.
when_not_to_use: As evidence that Nim beats C: with gcc as the backend Nim loses (Nim/GCC 1.10-1.14 s vs C/Gcc 1.02-1.047 s in every run from 2026-07-14 to 2026-10-05), and a hobby C compiler row (C/mycc/LLVM/Default, 1.026 s) also beats C/Gcc. The spread between equivalent C sources is about 15 percent.
Expecting -d:danger or -Ofast -march=native to add speed: on this test they are slower (Nim/Clang/Danger 1.114 s, Nim/Clang/Max 1.231 s, Nim/GCC/Max 1.41 s).
Floating-point or larger numeric kernels: in the same run Nim/Clang is slower than C/Gcc on CLBG::Nbody (1.73 vs 1.465 s), CLBG::Spectralnorm (1.011 vs 0.925 s) and Matmul::Single (8.788 vs 5.019 s).
The real CLBG fannkuch-redux workload (n=12, multithreaded, SIMD reference programs): only n=8, single-threaded and fully cache-resident, was measured.
Anyone needing a large margin: 1.13x over C/Gcc, below the V/Clang row (0.875 s) on the same test.

integration.dependencies: Nim 2.2.12 compiler plus clang (the LLVM 22.1.8 release tarball in the measured image); the kernel uses only Nim's system module
integration.min_toolchain: Nim 2.2.12 with clang 22.1.8 as measured (the nimble file requires nim >= 2.0.0); other versions were not measured, and the result depends on backend codegen
integration.platforms: Measured on x86-64 Linux (AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 78 GB) in Docker images built FROM ubuntu:26.04; the Nim build targets generic x86-64 (no -march=native)
integration.thread_safety: Not applicable: single-threaded pure function over stack arrays

gotchas: The result depends on the backend: the same Nim source is 0.918 s through clang but 1.116 s through gcc 16, slower than the hand-written C/Gcc row (1.036 s). This pattern held in all five runs checked, and the V/GCC row (1.126 s) shows the same reversal, so read it as clang codegen on Nim-emitted C, not as a Nim property.

Turning safety checks off makes it slower: Nim/Clang/Danger runs 1.114-1.146 s against 0.918-0.933 s checked across five runs. Similarly, C at -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops (1.278-1.364 s) loses to C at -O2 (1.036-1.174 s). On loops this short, extra unrolling or vectorisation costs time.

The three baselines are not line for line. C uses a runtime-length memcpy and a pointer swap helper, and C++ uses std::copy, std::reverse and std::rotate, so the C++ rows also measure library-algorithm codegen. Nim's arrays hold 64-bit ints where C and C++ use 32-bit int.

There is one in-process timing per configuration per monthly run, with no variance reported. The C/C++ prod rows are -O2 with -fstack-protector-strong and frame pointers, while Nim's nim.cfg passes clang -O3 -fno-strict-aliasing; the -O3 and -ffast-math C/C++ rows also lose, though their -flto is passed only at link time and is therefore inert.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The V/Clang (0.875 s) and Zig ReleaseSafe (0.977 s) rows of this test show the same codegen effect with a larger or similar margin, and V also reverses with gcc. Cite this Nim row only for Nim on clang; when citing the test itself, prefer the V or Zig rows.
verified_claims_summary: LangArena's 2026-10-05 run on an AMD Ryzen 7 3800X timed 700 calls of fannkuch-redux(8). Nim 2.2.12 (nim c --threads:on -d:release --cc:clang; clang 22.1.8 -O3, bound and overflow checks on) took 0.918 s. C/Gcc prod (GCC 16.0.1 trunk, -O2 hardened) took 1.036 s and C/Clang prod 1.174 s, and the best -O3 C/C++ row, C++/Clang++/Unsafe, took 1.137 s. That is about 1.13x, 1.28x and 1.24x (derived from page data), with all checksums matching 135762480.
status_note: LangArena is an active MIT suite (41 stars, last commit 2026-10-08, monthly reruns), and the 80-line Nim file is copyable; the speedup is a backend-codegen effect that disappears with gcc or -d:danger, so the entry stays at tier C.
